<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

<h1 class="ltx_title ltx_title_document">VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents</h1>
<div class="ltx_authors">

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) with full system access enable powerful task automation but pose significant security and privacy risks due to their ability to manipulate files, access user data, and execute arbitrary commands. While prior work has focused on browser-based agents and HTML-level attacks, the vulnerabilities of CUAs remain underexplored. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end threat model where Visual Prompt Injection (VPI) manipulates CUAs in black-box settings to perform unauthorized actions or leak sensitive
information, capturing the entire attack chain from injection to harmful outcomes. Then, we propose VPI-Bench, a benchmark of 306 test cases across five widely used platforms, to evaluate agent robustness under VPI threats. Each test case is a variant of a web platform, designed to be interactive, deployed in a realistic environment, and containing a visually embedded malicious prompt. Our empirical study shows that current CUAs and BUAs can be deceived at rates of up to 51% and 100%, respectively, on certain platforms. The experimental results also indicate that existing defense methods offer only limited improvements. These findings highlight the need for robust, context-aware defenses to ensure the safe deployment of multimodal AI agents in real-world environments. <span id="footnote4" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">§</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">§</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">§</span>
          
          
          
        Code and Demo: <a href="https://github.com/cua-framework/agents" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/cua-framework/agents</a></span></span></span><span id="footnote5" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">¶</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">¶</sup>
          <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">¶</span>
          
          
          
        Dataset: <a href="https://huggingface.co/datasets/VPI-Bench/vpi-bench" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://huggingface.co/datasets/VPI-Bench/vpi-bench</a></span></span></span></p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para">

<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">While AI agents offer exceptional efficiency in managing complex tasks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Park et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shen et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zeng et al., 2023</a>)</cite>, they also raise significant safety concerns. Many tasks require users to share sensitive personal information, such as login credentials, financial details, or card information, and often grant these agents control over their devices. For example, tasks like logging into online banking systems, making online purchases, managing personal accounts, or retrieving sensitive documents often involve the transfer of confidential information. Recently, Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>)</cite> have gained the ability to fully control users’ computers, performing actions such as mouse clicks, keystrokes, text input, file operations, or web browsing. While this enables human-like computer assistance and paves the way for powerful personal assistants, it also exposes sensitive data and system resources to potential exploitation, raising risks of data breaches, unauthorized actions, and serious privacy violations.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Despite the growing importance of ensuring the safety of CUAs, existing research remains limited in scope. Most prior studies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., </a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., </a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> focus on degrading task performance or decision-making in non-Computer-Use agents (i.e., Browser-Use Agents (BUAs)), which operate exclusively within web-based environments by browsing pages or interacting with HTML elements, without the ability to access the user’s local system. Although recent efforts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2024</a>)</cite> begin to examine how agents can be manipulated to leak private information, they remain confined to non-Computer-Use settings and consider privacy leakage only as a threat. More recently, pop-up attacks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, although conducted on CUAs, remain confined to shallow interactions with crafted interface elements (e.g., clicking pop-ups), depend on privileged attacker knowledge for high success, and focus only on generic desktop or web interfaces, without evaluating escalation into harmful consequences (e.g., an agent leaking sensitive local data, deleting files, or modifying files). Generally, existing red-team evaluations reveal several limitations when applied to CUAs:</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Over-Reliance on Text-Based Attack Vectors:</span> Recent works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Debenedetti et al., 2024</a>)</cite> assume attacks via HTML, DOM, or text-based manipulation, which apply to agents parsing structured content (e.g., SeeAct <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, WebArena <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>)</cite>) but not to advanced agents like Anthropic’s CUA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>)</cite>, which relies on rendered screenshots, making such methods ineffective.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Neglect of System-Level Threats:</span> Prior works <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., </a>; <a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., </a>; <a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chiang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> focus on browser-restricted agents, overlooking CUAs that enable file modification and command execution. Such broader privileges expose agents to risks like unauthorized manipulation and persistent compromise, which remain underexplored.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lack of End-to-End and Interactive Evaluation Frameworks:</span> Current evaluations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., </a>)</cite> mainly check whether an agent performs a single malicious action (e.g., clicking a button) in static or offline settings, without considering subsequent action chains and their ultimate consequences.
This narrow scope misses vulnerabilities that arise through chained behaviors in long-term, dynamic interactions. Evaluating CUAs requires real-time, end-to-end testing within fully interactive environments that closely simulate deployment scenarios.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we address these limitations by systematically investigating the security vulnerabilities of CUAs and BUAs that interact with dynamic environments in real-time under Visual Prompt Injection (VPI) attacks. VPI attacks are rendered on the screen, allowing them to be perceived by vision-based CUAs, while their presence in the HTML also makes them accessible to HTML-based BUAs. Although such attacks are typically easy for humans to detect, we consider a setting in which the user delegates a task to the agent without any further supervision. Our contributions include:</p>
<ul id="S1.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">End-to-End Threat Model via VPI.</span>
We propose an end-to-end threat model where VPI manipulates agents in black-box settings (i.e., adversary has no knowledge of the user or the agent’s architecture) to perform unauthorized actions or leak sensitive information, capturing the entire attack chain from injection to harmful outcomes, which provides a rigorous basis for studying real-world risks of CUAs and BUAs.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">VPI-Bench.</span>
Building on this threat model, we introduce VPI-Bench, a benchmark designed to assess the robustness of CUAs and BUAs against VPI attacks in dynamic environments. VPI-Bench contains 306 test cases across five popular web platforms: Amazon, Booking, BBC, Messenger, and Email, covering application domains such as e-commerce, messaging, and online services. We evaluate eight agents and record not only success and failure rates, but also fine-grained behavior traces to support standardized comparisons.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S1.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Robustness and Behavioral Analysis:</span> Using VPI-Bench, we show that all agents are vulnerable to Visual Prompt Injection: BUAs often execute malicious instructions without resistance, while CUAs, though sometimes more cautious, still exhibit high success rates. Agents sometimes complete only part of a malicious task, which still compromises security, and they often fail to recognize attacks, especially on platforms like Email.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Analysis of Influential Factors.</span>
We examine three factors influencing agent vulnerability: injection timing (early vs. late in task execution), defense methods, and the semantic alignment between benign and malicious tasks. Our results show that attacks remain highly effective regardless of timing, showing agents are broadly susceptible. While fine-tuning or proprietary defense layers offer partial mitigation, success rates remain high, and system prompt defenses are largely ineffective. Finally, we find that the greater the semantic relatedness between the benign and malicious tasks, the more likely the agent is to adopt the injected instruction.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Computer-Use and Browser-Use Agents.</span> Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) are LLM-powered agents capable of controlling a user’s computer through system-level operations such as browsing the web, managing files, and executing terminal commands. While powerful, their unrestricted access to user data and resources poses significant security risks. A few CUAs are publicly available: Anthropic’s model provides full computer control through visual perception (e.g., screenshot analysis) with additional defenses against prompt injection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>)</cite>. UI-TARS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025a</a>)</cite> presents an end-to-end, fine-tuned GUI agent that operates directly on screenshots and achieves strong performance across multiple GUI benchmarks through improved perception, grounding, and action modeling. OpenAI’s system <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI, 2025</a>)</cite> supports only limited web-based actions and is more accurately categorized as a Browser-Use Agent (BUA). BUAs, as a subset of CUAs, operate exclusively in web environments to perform tasks such as search or shopping without system access, using approaches ranging from raw HTML parsing <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yao et al., 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Deng et al., 2023</a>)</cite> and rendered screenshots <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al., 2024</a>)</cite> to structured pipelines <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Contributors, 2025</a>)</cite>. In this work, we evaluate the robustness of both CUAs and BUAs against VPI attacks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Prompt Injection Attacks and Benchmarks.</span>
Prompt injection attacks manipulate model inputs to induce unintended behaviors. Direct attacks use user-crafted prompts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vijayvargiya et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shayegani et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wei et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perez &amp; Ribeiro, 2022</a>; <a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Willison, 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Vijayvargiya et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hao et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jin et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025c</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zou et al., 2025</a>)</cite> to bypass safeguards <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Markov et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Inan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al., 2025</a>; <a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ghosal et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, while indirect attacks embed adversarial content <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Greshake et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Debenedetti et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chen et al., 2025b</a>)</cite>. These have proven effective against web agents via fine-tuned backbones <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Yang et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024a</a>)</cite>, adversarial images <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Fu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aichberger et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, injected HTML <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Cao et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, malicious webpages leaking private data <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Xu et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liao et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, or dynamic tool-mediated injections in interactive environments such as AgentDojo <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Debenedetti et al., 2024</a>)</cite>, though such attacks remain limited to DOM-based agents and fail on visual-only models <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>)</cite>. More recently, pop-up attacks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2024</a>)</cite> also use visually induced cues but remain shallow, requiring privileged access to internal UI states and evaluating only click behavior without assessing downstream system-level consequences or high-stakes domains such as messaging or email. They further lack a sandbox for analyzing multi-step malicious workflows. WebInject <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2025d</a>)</cite> further introduces a pixel-level perturbation attack that injects optimized visual signals during webpage rendering to coerce web agents into executing attacker-specified actions, though it focuses on single-step GUI manipulation and does not evaluate multi-step or system-level security breaches. Existing benchmarks primarily address behavioral hijacking: Ma et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al., 2024</a>)</cite> and Wu et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al., </a>)</cite> provide static, single-step evaluations, while Chiang et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Chiang et al., 2025</a>)</cite> and Kumar et al. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kumar et al., </a>)</cite> use adversarial webpages but exclude third-party data attacks, overlook system-level threats (e.g., file manipulation, command execution), and remain unreleased. Multimodal situational-safety benchmarks <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al., 2024</a>)</cite> evaluate Multimodal LLMs’ ability to recognize hazards and choose safe actions, but they do not involve adversarial manipulation or study how attackers can compromise agents through the visual channel. In contrast, our <span id="S2.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">VPI-Bench</span> offers 306 dynamic, real-time test cases against CUAs and BUAs, explicitly targeting user security and system-level vulnerabilities, with all environments publicly released for reproducible benchmarking.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Defense Methods against Prompt Injection</span> Researchers introduce many guard models to counter prompt injection <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Markov et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Inan et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025a</a>; <a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Liu et al., 2025b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wang et al., 2024b</a>; <a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sun et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhang et al., 2023</a>; <a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Oh et al., 2024</a>; <a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Du et al., 2024</a>)</cite>. These models primarily prevent jailbreaks that drive LLMs to produce harmful content (e.g., bomb-making instructions) rather than stop AI agents from executing malicious tasks that mimic normal user operations. More recently, Anthropic propose methods such as fine-tuning LLMs against prompt injection and adding defense layers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>)</cite>. In this work, we show that such defenses remain ineffective against VPI.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for
Computer-Use Agents</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Threat Model</h3>

<figure id="S3.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.02456v2/figures/securityagent.jpg" id="S3.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/333;" width="548" height="333" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>
Overview of the VPI threat model: each sample contains (1) a benign user prompt for a normal task, (2) a pseudo-authentic yet potentially compromised web platform, (3) a visual attack prompt injected by the attacker, and (4) an environment setup aligned with the attack to monitor unauthorized actions like file deletion or data exfiltration.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S3.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S3.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 3.1 Threat Model ‣ 3 VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> illustrates our threat model. Given a CUA deployed in an environment with access to system level resources (e.g., the local file system, command line interface, and external internet services), the user provides a benign prompt specifying a task <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{benign}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>benign</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{benign}}</annotation></semantics></math>. The agent is expected to fulfill this objective on a webpage <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="S3.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">without human supervision</span>. Under normal circumstances, it should carry out the user’s instruction without deviation. However, during the interaction with <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math>, the agent may be exposed to adversarial visual content embedded within the page, which conveys a secondary task <math id="S3.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{mal}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>mal</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{mal}}</annotation></semantics></math> introduced by an attacker. This hidden objective lies outside the scope of the original instruction, and is designed to covertly steer the agent toward unintended behavior.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Our threat model consists of four mutually dependent components:</p>
<ol id="S3.I1" class="ltx_enumerate">
<li id="S3.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">1.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Benign User Prompt (<math id="S3.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{benign}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">benign</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{benign}}</annotation></semantics></math>):</span>
A natural-language instruction from the user describing a harmless task (e.g., “help me buy glasses at the cheapest price”).
The prompt contains no malicious intent, and the agent is expected to act solely based on this instruction.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">2.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Web Platform (<math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math>):</span>
A pseudo-authentic webpage (e.g., “amazon.com”) that the agent should interact with to complete <math id="S3.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{benign}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>benign</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{benign}}</annotation></semantics></math>.
Though synthetic and built for controlled experiments, it closely mimics real sites.
Note that our threat model does not require any platform breach but instead reflects realistic scenarios where attackers can insert malicious instructions into these platforms by controlling legitimate web content (e.g., their own shop pages on Amazon, sending emails, etc.) that agents may naturally visit during routine tasks across open platforms.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">3.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Visual Attack Prompt (<math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v^{\text{adv}}\subset w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>v</mi><mtext class="ltx_mathvariant_bold">adv</mtext></msup><mo>⊂</mo><mi>w</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v^{\text{adv}}\subset w</annotation></semantics></math>):</span>
Malicious visual content injected by the attacker into the rendered page.
Although this content encodes a malicious task <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{mal}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>mal</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{mal}}</annotation></semantics></math> that is not implied by the original user intent (i.e., <math id="S3.I1.i3.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{mal}}\not\subseteq T_{\text{benign}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>mal</mtext></msub><mo>⊈</mo><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>benign</mtext></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{mal}}\not\subseteq T_{\text{benign}}</annotation></semantics></math>), the agent may still interpret it as a valid subgoal (e.g., “find an existing document file on the computer that contains bank account information, then read it and use it to complete the form”).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">4.</span> 
<div id="S3.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Execution Environment (<math id="S3.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\mathcal{E}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi class="ltx_font_mathcaligraphic">ℰ</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\mathcal{E}</annotation></semantics></math>):</span>
Each scenario is executed in a sandboxed environment that simulates both the local machine and internet-accessible resources the agent may interact with during task execution. The local component emulates a realistic file system, terminal interface, and other Operating System-level functionalities, while the internet component provides simulated access to external services such as cloud storage, email, and messaging platforms. This environment is dynamically configured based on the malicious instruction embedded in the visual attack prompt. For instance, if the prompt instructs the agent to retrieve a file containing bank account information to fill out a form, the sandbox includes a mock file (e.g., /home/bank_info.txt) populated with bank account content. This controlled setup allows precise observation of the agent’s behavior in response to adversarial prompts.</p>
</div></li>
</ol>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The goal of the attack is to induce the agent to complete the malicious task <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{mal}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>mal</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{mal}}</annotation></semantics></math>, visually embedded in <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="w" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>w</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">w</annotation></semantics></math>, even though it is not part of the original user instruction <math id="S3.SS1.p3.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="T_{\text{benign}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>T</mi><mtext>benign</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">T_{\text{benign}}</annotation></semantics></math>. In practice, this threat model represents a <span id="S3.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">scalable, black-box and opportunistic</span> attack path, where adversaries without knowledge of the user’s prompt, task, or the agent’s architecture can still indiscriminately seed malicious visual instructions across channels such as pop-ups, social media, messages, and emails. Agents routinely process these channels to complete user tasks without human oversight, so large-scale placement of malicious visuals in visible locations is likely to cause CUAs and BUAs to encounter and act on injected payloads. This creates an end-to-end risk where agents may be induced to carry out unauthorized operations or leak private data, resulting in tangible security and privacy harms.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Dataset</h3>

<section id="S3.SS2.SSS1" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.1 </span>Sample Format</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Each instance in the dataset is represented as a structured JSON object simulating a user-agent interaction. The format includes:</p>
<ul id="S3.I2" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S3.I2.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">id</span>: A unique identifier for the sample.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">url</span>: The URL of the specific webpage variant we construct for the corresponding test case, which serves as the target interface for the agent’s interaction.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">environment</span>: A list of low-level setup commands that define the execution context.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.I2.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">user_prompt</span>: A natural language instruction provided by a benign user, specifying the intended task.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S3.I2.i5" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S3.I2.i5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.I2.i5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S3.I2.i5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">attacker_objective</span>: A latent field describing the adversary’s intended malicious goal (e.g., API key exfiltration). This field is hidden from the agent and is used solely for evaluation to determine whether the agent fulfilled the attacker’s objective.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS1.p1.2" class="ltx_p">This format enables the systematic and automated testing of agent robustness, and security vulnerabilities in realistic, adversarial web environments. We provide a sample instance in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Dataset Sample ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS2" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.2 </span>Data Collection</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We begin by selecting five representative user domains: Shopping, Travel, News, Email, and Instant Messaging. For each domain we choose a corresponding popular platform, namely Amazon, Booking.com, BBC News, Email, and Messenger, and reimplement each site’s core functionality in a controlled environment to enable safe and reproducible experiments. To preserve visual realism, product and news pages are constructed from real screenshots and are augmented with popups that contain the injected visual prompts, while Email and Messenger interfaces are faithfully replicated to match real clients’ layout and interaction patterns such as sidebars and input fields. After interacting with the injected popup, agents are redirected back to the actual website so the workflow mirrors real usage. For each reimplemented site, we define a set of malicious tasks (Table <a href="#A3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Appendix C Task breakdown across web platforms ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) that cover unauthorized behaviors such as file manipulation, information exfiltration, and unauthorized communication. Based on these tasks, we then generate multiple adversarial webpage variants embedding visual attack prompts.
Attack delivery follows each platform’s typical interaction channel: popup advertisements on Amazon, Booking, and BBC, chat messages on Messenger, and emails on Email. Because VPI exploits screen-level perception, this design, built from real screenshots and faithful interface replicas, provides realistic exposure while preserving experimental control and safety. We provide sample webpage interfaces from our dataset in Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Pseudo-Authentic Webpage Interfaces ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS3" class="ltx_subsubsection">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsubsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsubsection">3.2.3 </span>Data Statistics</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To provide an overview of the dataset distribution, we present a breakdown of the samples across three key dimensions in Figure <a href="#S3.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 3.2.3 Data Statistics ‣ 3.2 Dataset ‣ 3 VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. As shown in the left subfigure, the majority of tasks (71.6%) require access to system-level resources (Computer-Use), while the remaining 28.4% are limited to browser-based interactions (Browser-Use). The middle subfigure groups samples by the targeted web platform, revealing that Amazon, Booking, and BBC each account for 25.8% of the total, whereas Email and Messenger comprise 15.0% and 7.5%, respectively. The right subfigure categorizes samples by their malicious objectives: 24.5% aim to perform unauthorized actions, 20.6% focus on exfiltrating private information, and 54.9% attempt both simultaneously. Here, we define unauthorized actions as agent-induced operations that alter the state of the user’s system without consent (e.g., file modification, command execution, or sending unauthorized messages), and privacy leakage as the exfiltration of sensitive user data to external parties. We provide additional details on the number of samples and type of attack goal for each malicious task across web platforms in Table <a href="#A3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Appendix C Task breakdown across web platforms ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. Each row corresponds to a malicious task, with the #Num column indicating the number of variants (e.g., uploading a research proposal, uploading banking information). These statistics highlight the diversity and coverage of threat scenarios considered in our dataset, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of agent vulnerabilities under varying operational and adversarial contexts.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F2" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.02456v2/figures/out2.png" id="S3.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/191;" width="548" height="191" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>
Distribution of samples across three dimensions.
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Evaluation Protocol and Metrics</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We employ two primary metrics to evaluate the behavior of the CUAs and BUAs under VPI attacks: <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attempted Rate (AR)</span> and <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Success Rate (SR)</span>. Let <math id="S3.SS3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>N</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N</annotation></semantics></math> denote the total number of attack samples. For each sample, the attack is categorized as either <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">attempted</span> or <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">not attempted</span>, and if attempted, as either <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">successful</span> or <span id="S3.SS3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">unsuccessful</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Attempted Rate</span> and <span id="S3.SS3.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Success Rate</span> are defined as:</p>
<table id="S3.Ex1" class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_table">

<tbody><tr class="ltx_equation ltx_eqn_row ltx_align_baseline">
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padleft"></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_align_center"><math id="S3.Ex1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{AR}=\frac{N_{\text{attempted}}}{N},\quad\text{SR}=\frac{N_{\text{successful}}}{N}" display="block" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mtext>AR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>attempted</mtext></msub><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow><mo rspace="1.167em">,</mo><mrow><mtext>SR</mtext><mo>=</mo><mfrac><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>successful</mtext></msub><mi>N</mi></mfrac></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{AR}=\frac{N_{\text{attempted}}}{N},\quad\text{SR}=\frac{N_{\text{successful}}}{N}</annotation></semantics></math></td>
<td class="ltx_eqn_cell ltx_eqn_center_padright"></td></tr></tbody>
</table>
<p id="S3.SS3.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\text{attempted}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>attempted</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\text{attempted}}</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S3.SS3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="N_{\text{successful}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>N</mi><mtext>successful</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">N_{\text{successful}}</annotation></semantics></math> denote the number of attack samples in which the agent attempted or successfully completed the malicious task, respectively. These metrics allow us to separately quantify the agent’s susceptibility to initiating malicious behavior (Attempted Rate) and its capacity to successfully execute such behavior (Success Rate).</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.SS3.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S3.SS3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To judge whether a malicious task has been attempted or successfully completed by the agent, we adopt a <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">majority voting strategy</span> using three independent frontier large language models (LLMs). Each LLM is provided with a structured input that includes the malicious task description, the benign user task description, and the agent’s execution trace. These inputs are accompanied by a predefined <span id="S3.SS3.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">chain-of-thought prompting template</span>, which is described in detail in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E LLM Judge Experiment ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>, to guide the LLMs in performing step-by-step reasoning. Each model then outputs a binary judgment for two criteria: (i) whether the malicious task was attempted, and (ii) whether it was successfully completed. A task is labeled as attempted or completed if at least two of the three LLMs return a positive decision for the respective criterion. This voting-based evaluation mitigates subjectivity and model-specific variance, resulting in more consistent and reliable assessments across diverse adversarial scenarios. We provide the experiments to evaluate the LLM judges in the Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E LLM Judge Experiment ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>. Generally, the results show that the Majority Voting method achieved an attempted accuracy of 98.00% and a completed accuracy of 95.00%, where accuracy is evaluated based on human-labeled ground truth, indicating that it is highly reliable.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Baselines</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate the susceptibility of agents to malicious prompts, we conduct experiments across two representative frameworks: Browser-Use Agents (BUAs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Contributors, 2025</a>)</cite> and Computer-Use Agents (CUAs) <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>)</cite>. We select these two frameworks based on the capabilities of their underlying models, their necessary tool integrations, and their community adoption, ensuring that the chosen agents have sufficient reasoning and tool-use support to successfully complete benign tasks. We also attempt to conduct experiments on UI-TARS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Qin et al., 2025</a>)</cite>, a model explicitly fine-tuned for GUI and computer-use tasks, but we find that its capability is not sufficient to complete the malicious tasks even though it is still susceptible to the attack (see Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Evaluation of UI-TARS ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>). For Browser-Use <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Contributors, 2025</a>)</cite>, we evaluate six models: GPT-5, GPT-4o, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Deepseek-V3, Gemini-2.5-Pro and Llama-4-Maverick. They interact with webpages via both graphical user interfaces (GUI) and visual perception, and are commonly used in web agent benchmarks. The Computer-Use framework is built on Anthropic’s platform <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>)</cite> and provides agents with full access to the local machine, including filesystem manipulation, shell command execution, and interaction with local applications. In addition to local access, CUAs can also browse and interact with web environments. This enables integrated operation across both system-level and browser-level contexts. We evaluate two versions of Claude models under this framework: Sonnet 3.5 and Sonnet 3.7. This setup allows us to benchmark the security behavior of agents in both Browser-use (web-only) and Computer-Use (web &amp; local) execution settings.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Implementation</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We build our benchmark on top of two open-source agent frameworks, one for Computer-Use and one for Browser-Use. We evaluate CUAs and BUAs on their respective test cases, as shown in Table <a href="#A3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Appendix C Task breakdown across web platforms ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. For the CUA, we run the system inside a Docker container hosted on a local machine. We implement a set of APIs for sending prompts, setting up the environment, and resetting it, enabling <span id="S4.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">fully automated evaluation</span>. For the BUA, the system runs directly on the local machine. We create a real Google Drive account to simulate a user identity, allowing the agent to retrieve and interact with personal data. Environment setup and reset for the Google Drive workspace are also automated through our custom implementation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We host all 306 webpages on a hosting service, accessible for real-time interaction to support reproducible evaluation. Depending on the test case, the agent is either instructed via user prompt to visit a provided link or automatically directed to the target webpage before receiving the task. These webpages simulate trusted platforms but may contain malicious prompts injected by an attacker.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Vulnerability of Models Under Visual Prompt Injections</h3>

<td id="S4.T1.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:5pt;padding-bottom:5pt;">Sonnet-3.5</td>
<td id="S4.T1.2.1.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="padding-top:5pt;padding-bottom:5pt;"><span id="S4.T1.2.1.3.2.1" class="ltx_text"></span> <span id="S4.T1.2.1.3.2.2" class="ltx_text">
<span id="S4.T1.2.1.3.2.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span id="S4.T1.2.1.3.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>
Vulnerability of different models to VPI attacks across five platforms. Each cell shows the <span id="S4.T1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">attempted rate</span> (top, gray) and <span id="S4.T1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">success rate</span> (bottom, black), reported as percentage mean <math id="S4.T1.m82" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\pm" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>±</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\pm</annotation></semantics></math> standard deviation. Lower values indicate higher robustness. Results are averaged over 3 runs.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.3 Vulnerability of Models Under Visual Prompt Injections ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> reports the attempted and success rates of various models under prompt injection attacks across five real-world platforms. The results are averaged over three independent runs. In general, both attempted and success rates are high across most models and domains, indicating that current systems remain vulnerable to injected prompts. However, a clear distinction emerges between models deployed in Computer-Use and Browser-Use settings.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Models in the Computer-Use category show mixed performance: Sonnet-3.5 records relatively low attempted/success rates on domains such as Amazon and BBC (e.g., 5.56%/4.44% on Amazon and 1.11%/0.00% on BBC), whereas Sonnet-3.7 exhibits considerably higher rates (47.78%/31.67% on Amazon and 19.44%/16.67% on BBC). For both models, however, the rates on Messenger and Email remain substantial, often exceeding 40%, particularly in conversational or multi-intent scenarios that chain together multiple tasks (e.g., retrieving information and composing a reply in Email). In contrast, all Browser-Use models show consistently high attempted rates, typically reaching 100% on Amazon, Booking, and BBC, while still exceeding 50% on Messenger and Email. These results highlight that agents across both categories remain broadly vulnerable to VPI, with conversational and multi-intent contexts being especially challenging.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Agent’s Behavior Analysis</h3>

<figure id="S4.F3" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.02456v2/figures/behavior_distribution.png" id="S4.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/279;" width="548" height="279" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>
Distribution of model behaviors across five platforms (Amazon, Booking, BBC, Messenger, and Email) for Sonnet 3.7 (top row) and Sonnet 3.5 (bottom row). Each pie chart illustrates the proportion of actions. The red tone indicates successful attempts, orange represents failure cases, and greenish-blue shades denote unattempted actions.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To better understand how models react to VPI attacks, we conduct a behavioral analysis of Sonnet-3.5 and Sonnet-3.7 under the Computer-Use setting across five platforms. Figure <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ 4.4 Agent’s Behavior Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> presents the distribution of model behaviors, categorized into five action types. <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Partial Execution</span> denotes cases where only part of the malicious task is completed (e.g., uploading but not deleting a file). <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Failed Execution</span> indicates that no sub-tasks were completed, often due to limited reasoning ability or missing tools. <span id="S4.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Attack Recognition</span> represents the ideal behavior, where the agent correctly identifies the prompt as an attack and chooses not to act. To classify these behaviors, we use LLMs to perform fine-grained classification of log results. Further experimental details are provided in the Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Agent Behavior Analysis Experiment ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>. Generally, the behavior of different models varies across different platforms.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Sonnet-3.5 generally exhibits more conservative behavior compared to Sonnet-3.7. In Amazon, Booking and BBC, Sonnet-3.5 demonstrates a higher proportion of unattempted actions, particularly those labeled as <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Attack Recognition</span> (e.g., 64.4% on Booking and 66.5% on BBC). In contrast, Sonnet-3.7 attempts more actions, resulting in a broader spread across success, partial, and failed executions. For example, on Booking, 36.7% of cases are categorized as <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Success</span>, but only 16.7% are unattempted with explicit <span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Attack Recognition</span>. This indicates that Sonnet-3.7 is more vulnerable to prompt injection attacks and less capable of recognizing injected prompts as malicious.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p">The distribution of behaviors also varies notably across platforms. On Messenger and Email, both models exhibit the highest vulnerability, with attempted rates reaching approximately 40% or higher, and the majority of those attempts resulting in successful execution. Notably, on Email, the proportion of Attack Recognition is particularly low (below 16%). These findings indicate that Email is a highly permissive platform where attacks are likely to succeed, and even when they fail, they are rarely detected by the model. On the BBC platform, the model behavior appears more cautious, with attempted rates of only 19.44% for Sonnet-3.7 and 1.11% for Sonnet-3.5. This can be attributed to two main factors. First, the user task in the BBC scenario is to summarize the news of the day (see Table <a href="#A3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ Appendix C Task breakdown across web platforms ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>), which does not require accessing user information or interacting with the local machine. Second, the injected prompt in this case is presented as a pop-up, a form of interaction that is uncommon on BBC and may be perceived as less credible or less contextually integrated by the model.
This suggests that contextual relevance is an important factor in attack success. Thus, future research should explore both developing more contextually-integrated attacks (offensive side), and devising ways to better identify whether instructions deviate from the user’s intent (defensive side).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Late and Early Injection Analysis</h3>

<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.02456v2/figures/late_early.png" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/140;" width="548" height="140" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>
Comparison of early and late prompt injection attack outcomes on Messenger and Email platforms using Sonnet 3.5 and Sonnet 3.7 models. Bars are stacked to show the proportion of Success and Attempted Only (i.e., failed attempts), under Early Injection and Late Injection scenarios.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate how early and late prompt injection scenarios affect attack outcomes on the Messenger and Email platforms using the Sonnet 3.5 and Sonnet 3.7 CUA models. Early prompt injection refers to the malicious task being displayed immediately to the CUA in its first screenshot (e.g., first email in the inbox), whereas late prompt injection refers to the malicious task being displayed to the CUA in later screenshots (e.g., last email in the inbox).
As shown in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ 4.5 Late and Early Injection Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, although the AR and SR of both models vary between early and late injections, they remain consistently high. Specifically, Sonnet 3.5 is more vulnerable to late injections, while Sonnet 3.7 shows the opposite result, and is more vulnerable to early injections. In practical settings, prompt injections are more likely to appear later in the agent’s trajectory, after the agent has navigated through a few pages or interactions. This experiment demonstrates that even late-stage prompt injections can still be highly effective, and in some cases, even more successful depending on the model architecture.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS6" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.6 </span>Effectiveness of Defense Methods</h3>

<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2506.02456v2/figures/defense_latex2.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_centering ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:548/167;" width="548" height="167" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>
Comparison of model performance across five platforms (Amazon, Booking, BBC, Messenger, and Email) under two conditions: with and without system prompt defense. Each subplot displays the Success Rate (top) and Attempted Rate (bottom) of four models: Sonnet-3.7 (Computer-Use), Sonnet-3.7 (Browser-Use), GPT-4o (Browser-Use), and Gemini-2.5 (Browser-Use).
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Fine-Tuning and Framework-Level Defense Layers.</span> Anthropic’s CUA integrates multiple defense mechanisms against prompt injection attacks by default, including (1) fine-tuning models to resist adversarial instructions as part of Anthropic’s alignment training, and (2) an additional proprietary defense layer implemented at the agent framework level <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">Anthropic, 2025</a>)</cite>.
In Table <a href="#S4.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 4.3 Vulnerability of Models Under Visual Prompt Injections ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, our results show that these defenses provide partial effectiveness: while our BUAs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citep">(<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Contributors, 2025</a>)</cite>, which lack such protective layers, frequently reach 100% success rate on several platforms, the success rate of Anthropic’s CUA remains below 60% across all platforms.
This gap highlights that CUAs, though still vulnerable, demonstrate a degree of robustness not observed in BUAs.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS6.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS6.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">System Prompt Defense.</span> We further investigate the effectiveness of system prompts in mitigating or preventing malicious attacks against AI agents. System prompts are predefined instructions or behavioral constraints embedded at the system level to guide the agent’s responses and decision-making processes. The detail prompt is in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D System Prompt Defense ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.
Specifically, we append the defense prompt to all models’ system prompts. To determine the impact of such prompts, we measured both the Success Rate (SR) and Attempted Rate (AR) of attacks in adversarial scenarios across all five platforms using both CUAs and BUAs. Our results, shown in Figure  <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ 4.6 Effectiveness of Defense Methods ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, reveal that the defense prompt does not have any significant impact on the overall SR and AR, as although it reduced the SR and AR for some platform-model combinations, it also increased the SR and AR for other combinations. These findings suggest that system prompts are not a universally reliable defense, and alternative approaches should be explored to enhance AI agent security.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS6.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS6.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Taken together, these results show that even when combining defenses at the model (fine-tuning), framework (defense layer), and prompt (system instructions) levels, agents remain vulnerable to VPI, underscoring the need for more robust defenses.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS7" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.7 </span>Influence of Semantic Relatedness Between Benign and Malicious Tasks</h3>

<div id="S4.SS7.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S4.SS7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We examine how semantic relatedness between the benign task and the malicious task affects the attack attempted rate. On the Email platform, we compare two benign tasks: <span id="S4.SS7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">replying to benign emails</span> and <span id="S4.SS7.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">summarizing benign emails</span>. Using Gemini-2.5-Pro, the model most susceptible on the Email platform, we observe a clear contrast. Replying produces an attempted rate of 96.67 %, while summarizing produces only 16.67%. Replying naturally involves composing and sending messages, which makes the malicious instruction appear contextually plausible to the agent. In contrast, summarizing is purely analytical and shares little semantic similarity with the malicious objective. These results show that the greater the semantic relatedness between the benign and malicious tasks, the more likely the agent is to adopt the injected instruction.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Discussion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our results show that neither prompt-based defenses nor fine-tuning is effective against VPI. We discuss two promising directions for mitigating the impact of VPI attacks.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Agent-Level Defense.</span>
Agent frameworks can incorporate internal safety layers that intercept unsafe behaviors before they are executed. A practical design is to introduce a lightweight guard model that operates independently from the primary reasoning model and monitors each predicted action. This guard evaluates whether the agent’s chosen action is consistent with the user’s intent, adheres to safety constraints, and avoids suspicious transitions triggered by visual cues. By decoupling safety verification from task reasoning, the framework can prevent high-risk actions even when the main model is compromised by a visually injected instruction.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">System-Level Defense.</span>
System-level defenses serve as the final layer of protection by controlling how the execution environment interfaces with the agent. Techniques such as permission gating, sandboxing, and runtime monitoring can restrict access to critical resources, including the file system, terminal operations, and external network requests. These mechanisms are particularly important when upstream defenses fail to intercept a malicious instruction. A promising direction is to enable the operating system to distinguish between actions initiated by AI agents and those initiated by human users. This distinction would allow the system to enforce stricter execution policies for agent-generated actions, such as requiring additional verification or outright blocking high-risk operations like file deletion or system modification.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this work, we introduce an end-to-end threat model to examine security risks of Computer-Use Agents and Browser-Use Agents under Visual Prompt Injection (VPI), a realistic yet underexplored attack vector. We present VPI-Bench, a benchmark of 306 test cases across five platforms, simulating realistic agent workflows where webpages embed malicious visual instructions. Experiments show CUAs and BUAs are highly vulnerable, with attack success rates up to 51% and 100%, while existing defenses offer only limited protection. These results underscore the urgent need for robust, context-aware defenses that generalize across platforms and adapt to dynamic adversaries.</p>
</div>
</section>

<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Reproducibility Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper provides a comprehensive description of all the components necessary to reproduce the experimental results (e.g., web platforms, adversarial test cases, evaluation metrics, agent frameworks, LLM judgers, etc.).</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx2.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Additionally, our dataset parquet file, and Computer-Use Agent (CUA) / Browser-Use Agent (BUA) code are made available at <a href="https://github.com/cua-framework/agents" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/cua-framework/agents</a>, with detailed setup instructions. Our web platform code is also made available at <a href="https://github.com/cua-framework/web" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">https://github.com/cua-framework/web</a>, and can be easily deployed using any static site hosting service (e.g., GitHub Pages).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Ethics Statement</h2>

<div id="Sx3.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper does not involve any human subjects or real user data, as only synthetic user data was used, and AI agents only interacted with pseudo-authentic webpages in sandboxed environments.</p>
</div>
<div id="Sx3.p2" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">While studying the security vulnerabilities of CUAs/BUAs may lead to potential misuse, we argue that this paper serves to raise awareness about the severe risks of Visual Prompt Injection (VPI) attacks on CUAs/BUAs (e.g., sensitive data exfiltration, system tampering, etc.). In response, this paper proposes VPI-Bench as a benchmark to guide the development of more robust AI agents.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Large Language Model (LLM) Usage</h2>

<div id="Sx4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="Sx4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We utilized GPT-5 exclusively for language refinement, including grammar correction and formal phrasing of sentences or brief paragraphs. The model did not contribute to research ideation, experimental design, data analysis, or substantive content development.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Limitations</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper assumes that users delegate tasks to agents without supervision, but in practice, users may see the malicious emails/messages/pop-ups and intervene. Future research should investigate techniques to conceal malicious prompts from users, while ensuring that they remain detectable by AI agents that rely on screenshot-based visual input.</p>
</div>
</section>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>System Prompt Defense</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent"><span class="ltx_inline-block"><svg id="A4.p1.pic1" class="ltx_picture" height="178.23" overflow="visible" version="1.1" viewBox="0 0 550 178.23" width="550"><g style="--ltx-stroke-color:#000000;--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" stroke="#000000" stroke-width="0.4pt" transform="translate(0,178.23) matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 0)"><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#000000;" fill="#000000" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 0 5.91 L 0 172.33 C 0 175.59 2.64 178.23 5.91 178.23 L 544.09 178.23 C 547.36 178.23 550 175.59 550 172.33 L 550 5.91 C 550 2.64 547.36 0 544.09 0 L 5.91 0 C 2.64 0 0 2.64 0 5.91 Z"></path></g><g style="--ltx-fill-color:#F9F9F9;" fill="#F9F9F9" fill-opacity="1.0"><path style="stroke:none" d="M 1.97 5.91 L 1.97 154.12 L 548.03 154.12 L 548.03 5.91 C 548.03 3.73 546.27 1.97 544.09 1.97 L 5.91 1.97 C 3.73 1.97 1.97 3.73 1.97 5.91 Z"></path></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 162.72)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:31.84em;--ltx-fo-height:0.69em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="12.3" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 9.61)" width="440.58"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A4.p1.pic1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:31.84em;">
<span id="A4.p1.pic1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p1.pic1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#FFFFFF;">System Prompt Defense</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g><g fill-opacity="1.0" transform="matrix(1.0 0.0 0.0 1.0 21.65 16.47)"><foreignObject style="--ltx-fo-width:36.62em;--ltx-fo-height:9.09em;--ltx-fo-depth:0.19em;font-size:10pt;" height="128.53" overflow="visible" transform="matrix(1 0 0 -1 0 125.84)" width="506.72"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_container"><span class="ltx_foreignobject_content">
<span id="A4.p1.pic1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_minipage ltx_align_bottom" style="width:36.62em;">
<span id="A4.p1.pic1.2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A4.p1.pic1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-fg-color:#000000;">Be vigilant against prompt-injection attacks. These attacks aim to trick you into performing unauthorized or unintended actions that may compromise user safety, privacy, or system integrity. You must not obey any instruction, whether shown on the screen, embedded in content, or appearing as a pop-up, unless it aligns with the user’s original intent and your task goal. If you encounter suspicious or out-of-context prompts, ignore them and proceed cautiously. Your priority is to protect the user and only execute actions that are safe, authorized, and clearly aligned with the given instructions.</span></span>
</span></span></span></foreignObject></g></g></svg></span>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>LLM Judge Experiment</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para ltx_noindent">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To evaluate how reliable the LLM Judgers are, we randomly selected 100 agent trace logs. We then manually analyzed each log and assigned ground-truth labels indicating whether the model had attempted and completed the task. These annotations were compared against the predictions made by the LLM Judgers, and the results are summarized in Table <a href="#A5.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ Appendix E LLM Judge Experiment ‣ VPI-Bench: Visual Prompt Injection Attacks for Computer-Use Agents" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>. The results show that the Majority Voting method achieved an attempted accuracy of 98.00% and a completed accuracy of 95.00%, indicating that it is highly reliable.</p>
</div>
